name: Salt-gradient organ seeding
subtitle: drawing cells deep into a lab-grown organ frame

effects.effect: cells in a liquid drift along a difference in dissolved salt

effect: cells in a liquid drift along a difference in dissolved salt
how: To grow a replacement liver or kidney, labs coat a spongy organ-shaped frame with a patient's cells, but the cells pile up on the outside and the core stays empty. Pumping fluid through the frame that is saltier at the centre than at the surface makes cells drift inward along the salt slope on their own, a few thousandths of a millimetre a second, filling the deep pores evenly within hours.
obstacle: Cells must tolerate the salt difference, and the pull is gentle, so very thick frames may still need channels to shorten the trip.
why: Uneven seeding is one of the walls between printed scaffolds and full-size organs.
real: Scaffold seeding is done by perfusion or capillary flow, and diffusiophoretic colloid deposition in hydrogels is studied, but nothing found on using solute gradients to draw cells into scaffolds.
